payload.name: Extract explicit first-person feelings about activities
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit first-person statement of the speaker's feelings or evaluation about an activity or experience, use this during extraction to create a preference/state candidate and during CRUD to store it.
content: During extraction: if the speaker explicitly states in first person how an activity or experience makes them feel (e.g., 'it's super exciting and free-feeling'), create exactly one candidate memory as a preference or state; do not infer feelings from third-party or generic statements.

During CRUD: store this candidate as a 'preference' or 'state' memory linked to the activity, with the source message and resolved timestamp; do not merge it into unrelated memories or expand it into additional searches.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that explicit first-person statements of the speaker's feelings or evaluations about an activity or experience are missed during extraction, so durable preference/state memories are never created. This applies to future sessions where a user or role-play speaker directly says how an activity makes them feel (e.g., 'it's super exciting and free-feeling'); it must not apply to third-party statements, inferred emotions, or generic observations without first-person affect.

payload.name: Extract_Explicit_User_Preference
payload.description: When a user explicitly states a favorite or strong preference (e.g., 'X is my favorite', 'Definitely X!'), during extraction, always create a preference candidate even if the message already produced other candidates.
content: During candidate extraction, if a user utterance contains an explicit first-person preference statement naming an item (e.g., 'Definitely X! It's my favorite'), always emit a preference memory candidate for that item, regardless of how many other candidates the message yields.
Do not require the preference to be the message's main topic; a clause or exclamation is sufficient.
Do not apply to hypotheticals, negated statements, or preferences expressed about other people.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that extraction can skip a clearly stated user preference when it appears in a message that already yielded other candidates or when it is phrased as an exclamation. The skill applies to any future session where a user explicitly names an item as their favorite or strongly preferred; it does not apply to implicit likes, negations, or statements about other people's preferences, where the base extraction judgment remains sufficient.

payload.name: Preserve_All_Stated_Preference_Reasons
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly gives multiple distinct reasons or qualities for liking or preferring something, and you are extracting or enriching a profile/preference memory, include every stated reason.
content: During extraction, read the full source message for all explicitly enumerated reasons or qualities attached to a preference (for example, phrases like 'because of X and Y' or 'it is A, B, and C').
Build the candidate content so each distinct stated reason appears; do not keep only the first, most salient, or most recent reason.
Stop after all reasons explicitly present in the message are captured; do not add implied or inferred reasons not stated by the speaker.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes stores only one of several explicitly stated reasons for a preference, leaving later questions about the omitted reason unanswerable. Apply when a message explicitly lists multiple distinct reasons/qualities for the same preference while extracting a profile/preference memory: capture every stated reason. Do not apply when only one reason is stated or other qualities are only implied.

payload.name: Preference-subject attribution from first-person cues
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message expresses a preference or opinion using first-person forms (I, my, love, enjoy) and another participant is mentioned in the session; ensure the memory subject is the speaker, not that other participant.
content: During extraction, if a message uses first-person evaluative forms ('I', 'my', 'I love', 'I enjoy') about a person, team, or thing, set the memory subject to the message's speaker. Do not reassign the subject to another participant only because that person was discussed earlier in the session or appears in the same commit window.

Before ADDing a preference/opinion memory, verify the subject field: if the message states the speaker's own view, the subject must be the speaker. Use a non-speaker subject only when the message explicitly describes that person's preference (e.g., 'Tim loves ...').

If a short reply (e.g., starting with 'Thanks!') continues the speaker's own evaluation, still attribute the memory to the speaker; do not let the addressee or a previously mentioned name override the speaker.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates can misattribute a first-person preference (e.g., 'I love his skills and leadership') to another participant mentioned elsewhere in the same session, creating a memory with the wrong subject. This skill applies when a message contains first-person evaluative cues about a person/team while another entity appears in the conversation context; it requires the memory subject to be the speaker. It does not apply when the message explicitly states a third party's preference.

payload.name: Extract Appreciation from Indirect Statements
payload.description: When a speaker makes an appreciative or positively evaluative statement about a subject, even phrased generally or reflectively, extract a preference/event memory for that speaker during construction.
content: During extraction: if a message contains an explicit appreciative or positively evaluative statement about a subject (e.g., 'Nature truly has a way of reminding us to appreciate the beauty around us'), create a candidate memory (preference or event) recording that the speaker appreciates that subject, even when the statement is not first-person or is phrased as a general reflection.

During CRUD: keep each speaker's appreciation as its own memory; if an appreciation memory for the same subject already exists for another speaker, ADD a separate memory for the current speaker rather than merging or skipping.

candidates.solves: Extraction skips indirect appreciative statements, so a speaker's appreciation is missing from memory. Applies when a speaker makes a reflective/general positive statement about a subject (e.g., nature) that another person has appreciated; record the speaker's own appreciation. Does not apply to messages that only describe a topic without evaluative language or that express someone else's appreciation.

payload.name: Extract attributes from casual ideal-description clauses
payload.description: When a user states an ideal, preferred, dream, or desired version of something in a short, directive, or parenthetical clause, extract each named attribute as a preference memory.
content: Scan every user message for attributes of an ideal, preferred, dream, or desired object even when the sentence is a short directive (e.g., 'Check my ideal X...') or an aside; do not skip the message just because its main intent is a request.
For each distinct attribute stated about that object, create a separate `preference` memory with subject equal to the user, citing the message evidence.
Stop after the attributes explicitly named in the clause; do not infer unstated features or expand into a list of possible preferences.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can skip a user's durable attribute when it is phrased in a short casual or directive clause (e.g., 'check my ideal X by the water') rather than in a full topical sentence, so the preference is never written to memory. The Skill applies when a future message names an ideal, preferred, dream, or desired version of something and lists attributes in terse or parenthetical wording. It does not apply when the user discusses a topic in full sentences, since default extraction already handles that.

payload.name: Extract attributable principle statements as preference memories
payload.description: When a message from an identifiable participant states a general belief, principle, or value judgment (e.g., 'X is the key to Y', 'the best way to ...'), create an extraction candidate for a preference/state memory attributed to that speaker.
content: During candidate extraction, whenever a message contains an explicit general statement from a participant about what is important, key, or best (e.g., 'is the key to', 'is important', 'the best way', 'should always'), create a preference/state candidate that preserves the claim and its speaker attribution.
Require the speaker to be identifiable in the message; do not extract impersonal world knowledge or generic advice that is not tied to a specific participant.
Stop after the principle is captured; do not also extract surrounding encouragement or small talk from the same message.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can silently omit statements where a participant asserts a general belief or principle, leaving no memory for later questions about what that person said. This Skill applies when a future session contains an attributable principle statement (e.g., 'X is the key to Y', 'the best way to ...') made by an identifiable participant, and ensures a candidate is created for a preference/state memory. It should not apply to impersonal world knowledge, pure small talk, or simple first-person preferences that the base extraction already captures.

payload.name: Extract coping and distraction preferences
payload.description: When a session message explicitly links an activity, object, or companion to helping the user cope, distract, or get through tough times, use during extraction to create a preference memory.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that something helps the user through tough times (e.g., 'helps when times get tough', 'nice distraction', 'great company'), create a preference memory for that activity, object, or companion, linked to the source message.
Do not apply to casual mentions of likes or hobbies without a coping or difficult-time context; default extraction handles those. Keep the memory evidence-bound and durable.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes misses explicitly stated coping or distraction preferences, so later questions asking what helps the user go unanswered. This Skill applies when a session message explicitly links an activity, object, or companion to helping the user through difficult times, and requires creating a preference memory for it. It must not apply to ordinary likes or hobby mentions without that coping frame, where the base extraction policy suffices.

payload.name: ExtractPreferenceFromPositiveExclamations
payload.description: When extracting candidates, if a speaker expresses a positive evaluation or exclamation about an object, place, or experience (e.g., 'X is so beautiful!'), create a durable preference memory for that speaker toward the evaluated thing.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit positive evaluative exclamations (e.g., 'so beautiful', 'love it', 'amazing') as evidence of the speaker's durable preference.
Create a `preference` candidate linking the speaker to the object of evaluation only when the statement expresses the speaker's own judgment, not a reported or hypothetical opinion.
Extract at most one preference per distinct evaluated object per message; stop once the preference is captured to avoid redundant candidates.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction fails to generate any candidate when a speaker states a durable preference as an exclamatory positive evaluation (e.g., 'The autumn colors are so beautiful!'), leaving the fact absent from memory. This applies to future sessions where a speaker makes an explicit first-person aesthetic or positive evaluation of an object, place, or experience. It does not apply to reported opinions of others, transient states, or explicit 'I like' statements that the base extraction policy already handles.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitPreferenceStatements
payload.description: When a user explicitly states a personal preference or favorite (e.g., 'I love', 'my favorite is') during extraction, create a preference memory candidate with qualifiers. Use when direct first-person positive preference phrasing appears, even amid other content.
content: During extraction, treat explicit first-person preference statements as mandatory candidates: phrases like 'I love', 'I like', 'my favorite is/are', 'I also love' should each yield a preference memory candidate.
Preserve qualifiers and category context in the candidate (e.g., 'dairy-free chocolate mousse' as a favorite dairy-free treat).
Do not skip a candidate because the message also contains questions or other topics; extract every distinct stated preference.
Do not create candidates from negations ('I don't like'), hypotheticals, or preferences stated about other people; if an identical preference memory already exists, merge/skip instead of duplicating.

candidates.solves: Extraction commonly omits explicit personal preference statements, so no durable memory is created and later questions about the user's favorites fail. Apply when a speaker uses direct first-person positive preference phrasing ('I love X', 'my favorite is X', 'I also love Y') in any message, and create a preference memory candidate, preserving qualifiers like 'dairy-free'. Do not apply to negations, hypotheticals, third-party preferences, or when the same preference memory already exists.

payload.name: Preference extraction from enjoyment statements
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states they love, enjoy, or are a big fan of an item or category, extract a `preference` memory capturing what they enjoy, and keep any recommendation in a separate `event` memory.
content: When a message contains an explicit positive affect statement ('I love', 'I enjoy', 'I am a big fan of') about an item or category, extract a `preference` memory for the speaker that states what they enjoy (e.g., enjoying books with adventures and magic), even if the same message also contains a recommendation.
Keep the recommendation, if present, in a separate `event` memory; do not let the event memory replace or absorb the preference statement.
Generalize to the category the speaker enjoys when the loved item exemplifies it (e.g., a book series with adventures and magic means the speaker enjoys those book genres).
Do not apply to messages lacking a stated affect (pure recommendations or actions) or to non-durable one-off states about a specific item.

candidates.solves: Construction agents lose explicit enjoyment when they store a statement like 'I love this series - it has adventures and magic' as only a recommendation event, so later questions about what the speaker enjoys cannot be answered. This Skill applies when a speaker explicitly states love/enjoyment of an item or category; extract a durable `preference` memory capturing that enjoyment and keep any recommendation as a separate `event`. It must not apply to messages that only describe actions (e.g., recommending) without an affect statement, or to one-off states about a single item.

payload.name: Capture preference intensity in media statements
payload.description: During construction extraction, when a speaker expresses strong affinity for a book or media item (e.g., 'favorite', 'really into', 'love'), record it as a preference with that intensity, not merely as a current activity.
content: When extracting from a message, detect explicit preference-intensity language about a book or media item (e.g., 'favorite', 'really into', 'love', 'obsessed with').
Create a preference memory that names the item and reflects the stated intensity (e.g., 'favorite is X' or 'really into X'); do not downgrade it to a neutral activity like 'currently reading'.

Use memory_kind 'preference' only when the statement conveys liking or degree of affinity. If the message only describes what someone is reading or doing without any liking cue, keep it as an event or state memory and do not add intensity.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes loses preference intensity: a statement like 'really into Sapiens' is summarized as 'currently reading', so later queries about favorites fail. This Skill applies when a user expresses strong affinity for a book or other media item using words like favorite, really into, love, or similar. It must not apply to statements that only describe reading or consuming an item without any liking or intensity cue, where the base policy already records a neutral activity or state.

payload.name: Extract explicit self-reported preferences
payload.description: When a participant explicitly states their own preference or favorite (e.g., 'my favorite X is Y', 'I love Z'), create a preference candidate during extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, recognize explicit self-reported preferences: phrases like 'my favorite ... is ...', 'I love ...', 'I enjoy ...', 'I like ...' (positive or negative). Create a `preference` candidate for the speaker, capturing the object and the source message. Do not require extra corroboration; the explicit statement is sufficient.
Do not extract preferences for other people, hypotheticals, or non-preference comments such as 'I have a lot going on'.

candidates.solves: The general problem is that explicit self-reported preferences in conversation are sometimes skipped during candidate extraction, so the fact never reaches memory. Apply in future sessions when a participant says in their own words what they like or dislike (e.g., 'my favorite X is Y', 'I love Z'), and create a preference candidate. Do not apply to hypothetical, negated, or third-party preference statements, which require additional evidence.
